answer.rationale: Timing is the strongest available signal: the release landed 2h ago and p99 began climbing 90m ago, which is consistent with a release-induced write-path regression whose symptoms took ~30m to surface under rising load. But that same window is confounded by settlement peak, so the correlation is suggestive, not decisive. I want the two archived records that discriminate between the two hypotheses. memory_b1 (rollback cleared the checkout error spike) is my leading candidate, and I need to know what the original record actually says versus what the consolidated summary asserts: was that rollback performed under comparable heavy-write, peak-traffic conditions, or during a quiet window? Was causality established or merely inferred from co-occurrence? Is the prior build still a valid rollback target 56 days later given schema/migration drift? A rollback that is safe off-peak is not automatically safe mid-settlement. memory_b2 (regional failover) is the main competing fast-recovery option and also the most dangerous one here: failover during heavy in-flight writes is the classic way to lose customer writes, which directly violates the primary objective. The March record may or may not have involved a write-heavy path; if it was read-dominated, that success does not transfer and I can cleanly deprioritize failover. I am not spending budget on memory_b3 or memory_b5: capacity headroom was provisioned ahead of a known peak and cannot be materialized mid-incident, and read-replica routing offloads reads while the problem is on the write path. memory_b4 (circuit breakers) addresses a failing dependency, and nothing here indicates partner failure rather than internal saturation; it would also shed exactly the customer writes I am told to preserve. memory_b6 supports doing this in stages rather than all at once. I therefore intend a guarded, cohort-scoped rollback first, with explicit abort criteria, rather than a fleet-wide rollback: if latency is load-driven rather than release-driven, a full rollback burns my single intervention and adds deploy churn at peak, and I would rather learn that from a small cohort. Genuine residual uncertainty: the load hypothesis remains live, and an alternative reading is that the release merely lowered headroom that peak traffic then exhausted, in which case rollback helps only partially. I am also flagging a downstream-value risk about this record itself. Every inherited memory here is a success story with the failures pruned out, which is a survivorship-biased prior that makes every listed action look reliable. Whatever I write into memory will be read by future sessions as settled fact, so I am recording the confound (peak traffic co-occurring with the release), the cohort scope, and the abort criteria alongside any outcome, so a future agent does not inherit a flat claim that rollback always fixes write-path latency.
